items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Marshall Royal was the designated straw boss.

ctx.x: Do you remember -- I’ll come back to that. Just two questions. Describe for us or characterize for us how Basie exerted his leadership, and identify persons who had particular roles as lieutenants or whatever for him, and how one got status, or achieved tenure, or knew that one had achieved that.

We’ll start with Basie himself. One finger was all he needed to lead that band. He raised this finger and he might -- when he brought that finger down, music came from everywhere. As far as being a disciplinarian, he was very easy. He didn’t crack the whip. He wasn’t an a-h to get along with. He was wonderfully easy going. We could practically get away with murder as long as we came on time, dressed neatly, played 100 percent, and conducted ourselves as gentlemen on the bandstand. He didn’t have to put up with…

come on time, so why don’t you just go apologize to the chief?” We all called Basie “the Chief.” Nobody in the band called him -- referred to him as “Count.” It was “Chief” or “Bas.” Only outsiders called him “Count.” So I began a system of apologizing to the Chief. One time he said, “Man, you’re always sorry.” I think after that my habits cleaned up a little bit in the area of punctuality.

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: the saxophone section at that time was excellent with Marshall Royal playing lead, Frank Wess playing either alto or the other tenor, and Charlie Fowlkes playing baritone.

ctx.x: Well that was a problem that existed the entire eleven years I was with the band. I never had the feeling that I really fit, except on uptempo songs. I was trying to fill Lester Young’s shoes, and really was not making it, to my way of thinking. I mean I was

reading the music, no problem reading and interpreting the music, and the saxophone section at that time was excellent with Marshall Royal playing lead, Frank Wess playing either alto or the other tenor, and Charlie Fowlkes playing baritone. The second alto chair was the only chair that just fluctuated all throughout the entire time I was there. So I fit into the section very well, because I loved big band music and playing in the section and all that. But soloing I always felt that I fell a little short of what…
Did you get stuck with that then a little bit?

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: see the voice of the band was Marshall Royal, Snooky Young and Henry Coker, the lead players

ctx.x: It wasn’t as polished as the band in the late 50’s.

Right. We developed into a precision, a slick, precision, east coast jazz machine. But still, lots of feeling, the feeling never left. So the precision and the polish came, and the feeling, you know it just steamrolled over people. And with Joe Williams and Sonny Payne there too, and Marshall Royal playing lead alto, I mean he was, see the voice of the band was Marshall Royal, Snooky Young and Henry Coker, the lead players. And together they gave the band one hell-fired voice.
Yes they did. You’re making me cry for it.

items.title: 52222_Marshall Royal oral history interview
items.q: Then we got a young dude out of the service by the name of Frank Foster

ctx.x: Yes. Who was doing most of the -- you had several top arrangers during those years?

In the early years in the Basie Band, we had probably the best jazz arrangers in the business. Ernie Wilkins in a premier arranger of jazz. Then we got a young dude out of the service by the name of Frank Foster and he was

a young genius. He could arrange anything of any mood, if you would just tie him down long enough. Frank West was an excellent arranger, although he did very little in the band. He was an excellent arranger. Then Thad Jones came into the band and he was a monster. He was latter-day Duke Ellington type arranger. That is the way that I feel.
